The job nobody wants

The accounts inbox is a queue of
questions you already know
the answer to.

  • Every chase is a manual lookup. Open the email, find the supplier, find the invoice, check whether it’s posted, paid, part-paid — or still in approval where the ledger can’t see it.
  • Statements are worse. A page of lines to tick off one at a time, and the ones that matter are the lines that aren’t there.
  • The answer lives in two places. Opera knows what’s settled. Your approval system knows what’s in flight. Neither alone can answer.
  • So it waits. Suppliers chase twice, someone promises to look into it, and the queue grows over month-end.
Inbox  ·  accounts@
Hi — can you tell me when INV70951 is being paid? It’s well past terms now.
Please find attached our statement to 31/07. Several items look unpaid on our side.
Following up on my email from last week regarding 9237…

Three questions. All answerable from data you already hold.

What it does

Three jobs, one inbox.

Reconciles statements

Reads the attachment, extracts the lines, matches them against the purchase ledger, and lists both sides of every discrepancy — including the ledger items the statement left off.

Answers payment queries

Works out where each invoice stands — settled, part-paid, still in approval, approved but not yet posted — and drafts the reply from that data.

Shows you the queue

Every statement, enquiry, supplier and aged balance in one place, with a daily digest of what has gone quiet and needs a person.

Workflow one

A statement arrives.

01

Recognised and de-duplicated

The sender is checked against your approved list. Redelivered or re-forwarded mail is spotted before anything else runs.

02

Lines extracted

References, dates and amounts read off the attachment — PDF, spreadsheet or body text.

03

Matched against the ledger

Each line matched to a purchase-ledger transaction, allowing for the reference formats suppliers actually use.

04

Both sides of the difference

Lines you have no record of, and ledger items the statement omitted. The second half is what manual checking usually misses.

05

Clean ones finish themselves

If every line reconciles and every invoice checks out across all connected systems, the supplier gets a per-invoice status report and the statement closes itself. Anything ambiguous is left as it is, for a person.

Workflow two

Someone asks about an invoice.

The reference is resolved, not guessed

References are pulled out of the subject and body, then each is looked up. A supplier writing “70951” for what you file as INV70951 is matched, not denied.

Opera is the book of record

If Opera says paid or part-paid, that wins — and the reply says when, how much and by what method, not just “it’s been paid”.

Approvals fill the gap Opera can’t

Not yet in the ledger doesn’t mean lost. Where an invoice sits in an approval queue, the reply says which stage.

Disagreement is never smoothed over

If the sources conflict, or one can’t be reached, nothing is sent. It goes to a person with the reason attached.

The vocabulary

“Unpaid” isn’t one thing.

Most friction with suppliers comes from answering a precise question with a vague word. APAssist distinguishes nine states, and says which one it is.

Settled — Opera is authoritative

postedpaid part-paidallocated

Read from the purchase ledger, with the payment date, amount and method behind it.

In flight — before it reaches the ledger

receivedin-approval approved-unpostedon-hold rejected

Read from your approval system, with the stage reached and who it’s waiting on.

And the honest one not-found

Nobody has it. Usually a wrong reference or the wrong supplier account — which is itself the useful reply, and far better than a confident denial.

Why you can let it reply

Is it safe to let AI email
your suppliers?

A fair thing to be cautious about. Four things stand between a draft and your supplier.

It only writes from data. The reply is drafted from the resolved invoice status, never from the model’s own recollection. No data means no draft.

grounded

Fixed checks reject known-bad claims. A draft that contradicts the ledger — saying unpaid while matching payments sit unallocated, or quoting a payment for something settled by credit note — is thrown out before sending.

checked

A second pass reads the finished draft. It asks whether the reply holds up against the data as a whole, to catch mistakes no fixed rule anticipated yet.

reviewed

Two switches, both off by default. Auto-send needs the company switch on and that individual supplier enabled. Until then every reply waits as a draft for one-click approve, edit or send.

gated

When any check fails the outcome is the same: the enquiry goes to a person with the reason recorded. The system is built to stop, not to have a go.

When nothing comes back

It chases the chase.

Reminder and escalation cycles

A statement query or enquiry that goes quiet doesn’t just sit there. It advances through reminder and escalation stages on your own intervals, until it’s answered or it lands on a person as needing action.

A daily digest, to your team

One scheduled email listing what’s overdue, what’s past its service level and what’s waiting on a decision. Deliberately internal — the digest never emails a supplier.

Hold rules you set

Conditions that stop automation for a supplier or a class of mail, so the cases you want a human on stay with a human, permanently and by rule rather than by memory.

Everything in the digest is also a screen you can work from.

The other half of the question

Who are we not paying,
and how late are we?

Read live from the ledger

Not a copy that drifts. The ageing is calculated from the purchase ledger at the moment you look, on the ageing period your company actually uses.

Joined up with the chasing

The same view shows which of those suppliers currently have an open enquiry or a query past its service level — so the oldest balance and the loudest supplier stop being two separate lists.

Useful before the phone rings

Aged balances are where tomorrow’s chase emails come from. Seeing them next to the enquiry queue is how you get ahead of them.

You stay in charge

Turn it on one supplier at a time.

  • Everything starts off. Install it and it watches, reconciles and shows you what it would have said. Nothing leaves the building until you say so.
  • Per-company switches. Auto-acknowledge, auto-reply and auto-complete are separate, and each is set per company.
  • Per-supplier opt-in. Enable automatic replies for the suppliers you trust it with, and leave the rest as drafts.
  • Strangers are quarantined. Mail from an address not on the supplier’s approved list is held for review, never processed automatically.
  • Nothing is sent twice. Redelivered mail is recognised, and every outbound message goes through one send path with a full log.
  • Roles. Administrator, Finance and Viewer, enforced in the interface and again on the server.

Nothing changes in Opera

APAssist reads the purchase ledger and updates its own records. It does not post, allocate or amend anything in Opera — by design, not by configuration. Your ledger cannot be changed by an email.

It never approves anything

Approval stays in your approval system. APAssist reports what stage an invoice has reached; it has no authority to move it.

Every action is audited

Who or what acted, on which company, through which channel, and the data the answer was based on — kept as a record, not a log line.

How it fits

Simple to deploy.
Nothing changes in Opera.

Opera SE & Opera 3
from one build

Both Opera platforms

Opera SE and Opera 3, from the same build. Multi-company throughout, with every record scoped to the company it belongs to.

Your inbox, either way

Point it at a dedicated accounts mailbox, or let your existing mail routing hand it the statements and payment chases while invoices carry on to your AP system.

Approval visibility is additive

Connect AP Automation and in-flight status appears in the answers. Leave it out and APAssist reports what the ledger knows, and says so — it doesn’t fail.

Degrades, never blocks

If an approval source can’t be reached, the settled answer from Opera still comes back, flagged as incomplete rather than presented as final.

Cloud or on-premise

Installed and updated like your other crakd.ai apps, with its own database, its own permissions, and the company switcher you already use.

Statements are filed

Every statement received is stored with the reconciliation that was run against it, so you can answer for a decision months later.

Being honest about what’s next

Built, and not yet built.

Everything on the previous slides is working today. These are named because the foundations are in place — not because they’re available.

Answer the phone as well as the inbox

The engine that resolves a status knows nothing about email, so a voice assistant can ask it the same question a supplier emails. Waiting on the voice platform itself.

deferred

Zahara and other procurement systems

In-flight status is read through a swappable connector, so adding a source is a connector rather than a rebuild. Designed, not built.

designed

Supplier contact records, onboarding and remittance advice

Present in the earlier supplier-automation tool and planned for APAssist, but not yet carried across. Approved-sender lists are in; the wider contact and remittance features are not.

not ported

A supplier portal

Self-service lookups instead of email. Deliberately parked — email covers the current requirement.

later

APAssist is at version 0.27 and in active development against live company data. We would rather show you the boundary than discover it together after you’ve bought.
